mn22:0.2: The Simile of the Water Snake
mn22:1.2: At one time, the Blessed One was dwelling in Sāvatthī at Jeta's Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
mn22:2.1: Now at that time, a monk named Ariṭṭha, formerly a vulture trainer, had given rise to this harmful wrong view:
mn22:2.2: “As I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, those things called obstructive by the Blessed One are not sufficient to obstruct one who engages in them.”
mn22:2.4: “It is said that the monk named Ariṭṭha, formerly a vulture trainer, has given rise to this harmful wrong view:
mn22:2.5: ‘As I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, those things called obstructive by the Blessed One are not sufficient to obstruct one who engages in them.’”
mn22:3.1: Then those monks approached the monk Ariṭṭha, formerly a vulture trainer; having approached, they said to the monk Ariṭṭha, formerly a vulture trainer:
mn22:3.2: “Is it true, friend Ariṭṭha, that such a harmful wrong view has arisen in you:
mn22:3.3: ‘As I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, those things called obstructive by the Blessed One are not sufficient to obstruct one who engages in them’?”
mn22:3.4: “Indeed, friends, I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One thus: those things called obstructive by the Blessed One are not sufficient to obstruct one who engages in them.”
mn22:3.5: Then those monks, desiring to dissuade the monk Ariṭṭha, formerly a vulture trainer, from that harmful wrong view, questioned him, cross-examined him, and admonished him:
mn22:3.6: “Do not say so, friend Ariṭṭha; do not misrepresent the Blessed One. It is not good to misrepresent the Blessed One, for the Blessed One would not say such a thing.
mn22:3.7: In many ways, friend Ariṭṭha, obstructive things have been declared obstructive by the Blessed One, and they are sufficient to obstruct one who engages in them.
mn22:3.8: Sensual pleasures have been declared by the Blessed One to be of little satisfaction, full of suffering, full of trouble, with even greater danger herein.
mn22:3.9: Sensual pleasures have been declared by the Blessed One to be like a skeleton …
mn22:3.10: Sensual pleasures have been declared by the Blessed One to be like a piece of meat …
mn22:3.11: Sensual pleasures have been declared by the Blessed One to be like a torch of grass …
mn22:3.12: Sensual pleasures have been declared by the Blessed One to be like a pit of burning coals …
mn22:3.13: Sensual pleasures have been declared by the Blessed One to be like a dream …
mn22:3.14: Sensual pleasures have been declared by the Blessed One to be like something borrowed …
mn22:3.15: Sensual pleasures have been declared by the Blessed One to be like the fruit of a tree …
mn22:3.16: Sensual pleasures have been declared by the Blessed One to be like a slaughterhouse …
mn22:3.17: Sensual pleasures have been declared by the Blessed One to be like a sword or spear …
mn22:3.18: Sensual pleasures have been declared by the Blessed One to be like a snake’s head, full of suffering, full of trouble, with even greater danger herein.”
mn22:3.19: Yet even so, the monk Ariṭṭha, formerly a vulture trainer, when questioned, cross-examined, and admonished by those monks, stubbornly clung to and persisted in that harmful wrong view, saying:
mn22:3.20: “Indeed, friends, I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One thus: those things called obstructive by the Blessed One are not sufficient to obstruct one who engages in them.”
mn22:3.21: When those monks were unable to dissuade the monk Ariṭṭha, formerly a vulture trainer, from that harmful wrong view, they approached the Blessed One; having approached, they paid homage to the Blessed One and sat to one side. Sitting to one side, those monks said to the Blessed One:
mn22:3.22: “Venerable sir, a harmful wrong view has arisen in the monk named Ariṭṭha, formerly a vulture trainer:
mn22:3.23: ‘As I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, those things called obstructive by the Blessed One are not sufficient to obstruct one who engages in them.’
mn22:3.25: ‘It is said that the monk named Ariṭṭha, formerly a vulture trainer, has given rise to this harmful wrong view—
mn22:3.26: As I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, those things called obstructive by the Blessed One are not sufficient to obstruct one who engages in them.’
mn22:3.27: Then we, venerable sir, approached the monk Ariṭṭha, formerly a vulture trainer; having approached, we said to the monk Ariṭṭha, formerly a vulture trainer:
mn22:3.28: ‘Is it true, friend Ariṭṭha, that such a harmful wrong view has arisen in you—
mn22:3.29: As I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, those things called obstructive by the Blessed One are not sufficient to obstruct one who engages in them’?”
mn22:3.30: When this was said, venerable sir, the monk Ariṭṭha, formerly a vulture trainer, said to us:
mn22:3.31: ‘Indeed, friends, I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One thus: those things called obstructive by the Blessed One are not sufficient to obstruct one who engages in them.’
mn22:3.32: Then we, venerable sir, desiring to dissuade the monk Ariṭṭha, formerly a vulture trainer, from that harmful wrong view, questioned him, cross-examined him, and admonished him:
mn22:3.33: ‘Do not say so, friend Ariṭṭha; do not misrepresent the Blessed One. It is not good to misrepresent the Blessed One, for the Blessed One would not say such a thing.
mn22:3.34: In many ways, friend Ariṭṭha, obstructive things have been declared obstructive by the Blessed One, and they are sufficient to obstruct one who engages in them.
mn22:3.35: Sensual pleasures have been declared by the Blessed One to be of little satisfaction, full of suffering, full of trouble, with even greater danger herein.
mn22:3.36: Sensual pleasures have been declared by the Blessed One to be like a skeleton …
mn22:3.37: Sensual pleasures have been declared by the Blessed One to be like a snake’s head, full of suffering, full of trouble, with even greater danger herein.’
mn22:3.38: Yet even so, venerable sir, the monk Ariṭṭha, formerly a vulture trainer, when questioned, cross-examined, and admonished by us, stubbornly clung to and persisted in that harmful wrong view, saying:
mn22:3.39: ‘Indeed, friends, I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One thus: those things called obstructive by the Blessed One are not sufficient to obstruct one who engages in them.’
mn22:4.1: When we, venerable sir, were unable to dissuade the monk Ariṭṭha, formerly a vulture trainer, from that harmful wrong view, we came to report this matter to the Blessed One.”
mn22:5.1: Then the Blessed One addressed a certain monk:
mn22:5.2: “Go, monk, and in my name summon the monk Ariṭṭha, formerly a vulture trainer, saying:
mn22:5.4: “Yes, venerable sir,” that monk replied to the Blessed One and approached the monk Ariṭṭha, formerly a vulture trainer; having approached, he said to the monk Ariṭṭha, formerly a vulture trainer:
mn22:5.6: “Yes, friend,” replied the monk Ariṭṭha, formerly a vulture trainer, to that monk, and he approached the Blessed One; having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat to one side. Sitting to one side, the Blessed One said to the monk Ariṭṭha, formerly a vulture trainer:
mn22:5.7: “Is it true, Ariṭṭha, that such a harmful wrong view has arisen in you:
mn22:5.8: ‘As I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, those things called obstructive by the Blessed One are not sufficient to obstruct one who engages in them’?”
mn22:5.9: “Indeed, venerable sir, I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One thus: ‘those things called obstructive by the Blessed One are not sufficient to obstruct one who engages in them.’”
mn22:6.1: “To whom, foolish man, do you understand that I have taught the Dhamma in this way?
mn22:6.2: Have I not, foolish man, declared in many ways that obstructive things are obstructive, and they are sufficient to obstruct one who engages in them?
mn22:6.3: Sensual pleasures have been declared by me to be of little satisfaction, full of suffering, full of trouble, with even greater danger herein.
mn22:6.4: Sensual pleasures have been declared by me to be like a skeleton …
mn22:6.5: Sensual pleasures have been declared by me to be like a piece of meat …
mn22:6.6: Sensual pleasures have been declared by me to be like a torch of grass …
mn22:6.7: Sensual pleasures have been declared by me to be like a pit of burning coals …
mn22:6.8: Sensual pleasures have been declared by me to be like a dream …
mn22:6.9: Sensual pleasures have been declared by me to be like something borrowed …
mn22:6.10: Sensual pleasures have been declared by me to be like the fruit of a tree …
mn22:6.11: Sensual pleasures have been declared by me to be like a slaughterhouse …
mn22:6.12: Sensual pleasures have been declared by me to be like a sword or spear …
mn22:6.13: Sensual pleasures have been declared by me to be like a snake’s head, full of suffering, full of trouble, with even greater danger herein.
mn22:6.14: Yet you, foolish man, by your wrong grasp of the teaching, misrepresent us, harm yourself, and generate much demerit.
mn22:6.15: This, foolish man, will lead to your harm and suffering for a long time.”
mn22:7.1: Then the Blessed One addressed the monks:
mn22:7.3: Has this monk Ariṭṭha, formerly a vulture trainer, even kindled a spark of understanding in this Dhamma and Discipline?”
mn22:7.6: When this was said, the monk Ariṭṭha, formerly a vulture trainer, sat silent, dismayed, with shoulders slumped, head down, brooding, and unable to respond.
mn22:7.7: Then the Blessed One, seeing the monk Ariṭṭha, formerly a vulture trainer, silent, dismayed, with shoulders slumped, head down, brooding, and unable to respond, said to him:
mn22:7.8: “You, foolish man, will be recognized by your own harmful wrong view.
mn22:7.9: Here, I will question the monks.”
mn22:8.1: Then the Blessed One addressed the monks:
mn22:8.2: “Do you too, monks, understand the Dhamma taught by me as this monk Ariṭṭha, formerly a vulture trainer, understands it, who by his wrong grasp misrepresents us, harms himself, and generates much demerit?”
mn22:8.4: For in many ways, venerable sir, obstructive things have been declared obstructive by the Blessed One, and they are sufficient to obstruct one who engages in them.
mn22:8.5: They are sufficient to obstruct one who engages in them.
mn22:8.6: Sensual pleasures have been declared by the Blessed One to be of little satisfaction, full of suffering, full of trouble, with even greater danger herein.
mn22:8.7: Sensual pleasures have been declared by the Blessed One to be like a skeleton …
mn22:8.8: Sensual pleasures have been declared by the Blessed One to be like a snake’s head, full of suffering, full of trouble, with even greater danger herein.”
mn22:8.9: “Good, good, monks! It is good that you understand the Dhamma taught by me thus.
mn22:8.10: For in many ways, monks, I have declared obstructive things to be obstructive, and they are sufficient to obstruct one who engages in them.
mn22:8.11: Sensual pleasures have been declared by me to be of little satisfaction, full of suffering, full of trouble, with even greater danger herein.
mn22:8.12: Sensual pleasures have been declared by me to be like a skeleton …
mn22:8.13: Sensual pleasures have been declared by me to be like a snake’s head, full of suffering, full of trouble, with even greater danger herein.
mn22:8.14: Yet this monk Ariṭṭha, formerly a vulture trainer, by his wrong grasp misrepresents us, harms himself, and generates much demerit.
mn22:8.15: This, for that foolish man, will lead to his harm and suffering for a long time.
mn22:9.1: Monks, that someone would indulge in sensual pleasures apart from sensual desires, apart from perceptions of sensual pleasures, apart from thoughts of sensual pleasures—this possibility does not exist.
mn22:10.1: Here, monks, some foolish people learn the Dhamma—
mn22:10.2: discourses, mixed prose and verse, expositions, verses, inspired utterances, sayings, birth stories, marvelous accounts, and dialogues.
mn22:10.3: Having learned that Dhamma, they do not examine the meaning of those teachings with wisdom.
mn22:10.4: Those teachings, not examined with wisdom for their meaning, do not lead to clear understanding.
mn22:10.5: They learn the Dhamma only for the sake of criticizing and for winning debates.
mn22:10.6: The purpose for which they learn the Dhamma, they do not experience that purpose.
mn22:10.7: Those teachings, wrongly grasped by them, lead to their harm and suffering for a long time.
mn22:10.9: Because of their wrong grasp of the teachings, monks.
mn22:10.10: Suppose, monks, a man seeking a snake, searching for a snake, wandering in pursuit of a snake.
mn22:10.11: He might see a large snake.
mn22:10.12: He might grasp it by its coils or tail.
mn22:10.13: That snake, turning back, might bite him on the hand, arm, or some other limb.
mn22:10.14: Because of this, he might meet with death or pain equivalent to death.
mn22:10.16: Because of his wrong grasp of the snake, monks.
mn22:10.17: In the same way, monks, here some foolish people learn the Dhamma—
mn22:10.18: discourses, mixed prose and verse, expositions, verses, inspired utterances, sayings, birth stories, marvelous accounts, and dialogues.
mn22:10.19: Having learned that Dhamma, they do not examine the meaning of those teachings with wisdom.
mn22:10.20: Those teachings, not examined with wisdom for their meaning, do not lead to clear understanding.
mn22:10.21: They learn the Dhamma only for the sake of criticizing and for winning debates.
mn22:10.22: The purpose for which they learn the Dhamma, they do not experience that purpose.
mn22:10.23: Those teachings, wrongly grasped by them, lead to their harm and suffering for a long time.
mn22:10.25: Because of their wrong grasp of the teachings, monks.
mn22:11.1: But here, monks, some noble sons learn the Dhamma—
mn22:11.2: discourses, mixed prose and verse, expositions, verses, inspired utterances, sayings, birth stories, marvelous accounts, and dialogues.
mn22:11.3: Having learned that Dhamma, they examine the meaning of those teachings with wisdom.
mn22:11.4: Those teachings, examined with wisdom for their meaning, lead to clear understanding.
mn22:11.5: They do not learn the Dhamma for the sake of criticizing or for winning debates.
mn22:11.6: The purpose for which they learn the Dhamma, they experience that purpose.
mn22:11.7: Those teachings, rightly grasped by them, lead to their benefit and happiness for a long time.
mn22:11.9: Because of their right grasp of the teachings, monks.
mn22:11.10: Suppose, monks, a man seeking a snake, searching for a snake, wandering in pursuit of a snake.
mn22:11.11: He might see a large snake.
mn22:11.12: He might firmly restrain it with a forked stick.
mn22:11.13: Having firmly restrained it with a forked stick, he might grasp it well by the neck.
mn22:11.14: Even if that snake, monks, were to wrap its coils around that man’s hand, arm, or some other limb, still he would not meet with death or pain equivalent to death because of it.
mn22:11.16: Because of his right grasp of the snake, monks.
mn22:11.17: In the same way, monks, here some noble sons learn the Dhamma—
mn22:11.18: discourses, mixed prose and verse, expositions, verses, inspired utterances, sayings, birth stories, marvelous accounts, and dialogues.
mn22:11.19: Having learned that Dhamma, they examine the meaning of those teachings with wisdom.
mn22:11.20: Those teachings, examined with wisdom for their meaning, lead to clear understanding.
mn22:11.21: They do not learn the Dhamma for the sake of criticizing or for winning debates.
mn22:11.22: The purpose for which they learn the Dhamma, they experience that purpose.
mn22:11.23: Those teachings, rightly grasped by them, lead to their benefit and happiness for a long time.
mn22:11.25: Because of their right grasp of the teachings, monks.
mn22:12.1: Therefore, monks, you should understand the meaning of what I have taught and hold it accordingly.
mn22:12.2: If you do not understand the meaning of what I have taught, you should question me about it or those monks who are learned.
mn22:13.1: Monks, I will teach you the Dhamma with the simile of a raft, for the purpose of crossing over, not for holding onto.
mn22:13.2: Listen and attend closely; I will speak.”
mn22:13.3: “Yes, venerable sir,” those monks replied to the Blessed One.
mn22:13.5: Suppose, monks, a man traveling along a road.
mn22:13.6: He might see a great expanse of water, with the near shore dangerous and frightening, and the far shore safe and free from danger;
mn22:13.7: but there is no boat for crossing or a bridge to go from one side to the other.
mn22:13.9: ‘This is a great expanse of water, with the near shore dangerous and frightening, and the far shore safe and free from danger;
mn22:13.10: but there is no boat for crossing or a bridge to go from one side to the other.
mn22:13.11: Suppose I gather grass, sticks, branches, and leaves, bind them into a raft, and, relying on that raft, using my hands and feet, safely cross to the far shore.’
mn22:13.12: Then, monks, that man, having gathered grass, sticks, branches, and leaves, and bound them into a raft, relying on that raft and using his hands and feet, might safely cross to the far shore.
mn22:13.13: Having crossed and reached the far shore, it might occur to that man:
mn22:13.14: ‘This raft has been very helpful to me;
mn22:13.15: relying on this raft, using my hands and feet, I safely crossed to the far shore.
mn22:13.16: Suppose I hoist this raft onto my head or carry it on my shoulder and go wherever I wish.’
mn22:13.18: Would that man, acting in this way, be doing what should be done with that raft?”
mn22:13.20: And how, monks, would that man be doing what should be done with that raft?
mn22:13.21: Here, monks, having crossed and reached the far shore, it might occur to that man:
mn22:13.22: ‘This raft has been very helpful to me;
mn22:13.23: relying on this raft, using my hands and feet, I safely crossed to the far shore.
mn22:13.24: Suppose I set this raft down on dry land or let it float away in the water and go wherever I wish.’
mn22:13.25: Acting in this way, monks, that man would be doing what should be done with that raft.
mn22:13.26: In the same way, monks, I have taught the Dhamma with the simile of a raft, for the purpose of crossing over, not for holding onto.
mn22:14.1: Monks, understanding the Dhamma as taught with the simile of a raft, you should let go even of the teachings, let alone what is not the teaching.
mn22:15.1: Monks, there are these six bases for views.
mn22:15.3: Here, monks, an uninstructed ordinary person, who has not seen the noble ones, is unskilled in the Dhamma of the noble ones, untrained in the Dhamma of the noble ones, who has not seen the good persons, is unskilled in the Dhamma of the good persons, untrained in the Dhamma of the good persons,
mn22:15.4: regards form as: ‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self’;
mn22:15.5: regards feeling as: ‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self’;
mn22:15.6: regards perception as: ‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self’;
mn22:15.7: regards formations as: ‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self’;
mn22:15.8: whatever is seen, heard, sensed, cognized, attained, sought after, or reflected upon by the mind, that too he regards as: ‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self’;
mn22:15.10: ‘This is the self, this is the world; after death I shall be permanent, lasting, eternal, not subject to change, and I shall remain thus forever’—
mn22:15.11: that too he regards as: ‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self.’
mn22:16.1: But a learned noble disciple, who has seen the noble ones, is skilled in the Dhamma of the noble ones, well-trained in the Dhamma of the noble ones, who has seen the good persons, is skilled in the Dhamma of the good persons, well-trained in the Dhamma of the good persons,
mn22:16.2: regards form as: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self’;
mn22:16.3: regards feeling as: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self’;
mn22:16.4: regards perception as: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self’;
mn22:16.5: regards formations as: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self’;
mn22:16.6: whatever is seen, heard, sensed, cognized, attained, sought after, or reflected upon by the mind, that too he regards as: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self’;
mn22:16.8: ‘This is the self, this is the world; after death I shall be permanent, lasting, eternal, not subject to change, and I shall remain thus forever’—
mn22:16.9: that too he regards as: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.’
mn22:17.1: Seeing thus, he does not become anxious about what does not exist.”
mn22:18.1: When this was said, a certain monk said to the Blessed One:
mn22:18.2: “Venerable sir, could there be anxiety about what does not exist externally?”
mn22:18.3: “There could be, monk,” the Blessed One said.
mn22:18.5: ‘It was mine, but now it is not mine;
mn22:18.6: it might be mine, but I do not obtain it.’
mn22:18.7: He sorrows, grieves, laments, beats his breast, and falls into confusion.
mn22:18.8: Thus, monk, there is anxiety about what does not exist externally.”
mn22:19.1: “But, venerable sir, could there be no anxiety about what does not exist externally?”
mn22:19.2: “There could be, monk,” the Blessed One said.
mn22:19.3: Here, monk, someone does not think thus:
mn22:19.4: ‘It was mine, but now it is not mine;
mn22:19.5: it might be mine, but I do not obtain it.’
mn22:19.6: He does not sorrow, grieve, lament, beat his breast, or fall into confusion.
mn22:19.7: Thus, monk, there is no anxiety about what does not exist externally.”
mn22:20.1: “Venerable sir, could there be anxiety about what does not exist internally?”
mn22:20.2: “There could be, monk,” the Blessed One said.
mn22:20.4: ‘This is the self, this is the world; after death I shall be permanent, lasting, eternal, not subject to change, and I shall remain thus forever.’
mn22:20.5: He hears the Tathāgata or a disciple of the Tathāgata teaching the Dhamma for the uprooting of all bases for views, determinations, obsessions, adherences, and underlying tendencies, for the stilling of all formations, for the relinquishment of all attachments, for the destruction of craving, for dispassion, for cessation, for Nibbāna.
mn22:20.7: ‘I will surely be annihilated, I will surely perish, I will surely cease to exist.’
mn22:20.8: He sorrows, grieves, laments, beats his breast, and falls into confusion.
mn22:20.9: Thus, monk, there is anxiety about what does not exist internally.”
mn22:21.1: “But, venerable sir, could there be no anxiety about what does not exist internally?”
mn22:21.2: “There could be, monk,” the Blessed One said.
mn22:21.3: “Here, monk, someone does not hold this view:
mn22:21.4: ‘This is the self, this is the world; after death I shall be permanent, lasting, eternal, not subject to change, and I shall remain thus forever.’
mn22:21.5: He hears the Tathāgata or a disciple of the Tathāgata teaching the Dhamma for the uprooting of all bases for views, determinations, obsessions, adherences, and underlying tendencies, for the stilling of all formations, for the relinquishment of all attachments, for the destruction of craving, for dispassion, for cessation, for Nibbāna.
mn22:21.6: It does not occur to him:
mn22:21.7: ‘I will surely be annihilated, I will surely perish, I will surely cease to exist.’
mn22:21.8: He does not sorrow, grieve, lament, beat his breast, or fall into confusion.
mn22:21.9: Thus, monk, there is no anxiety about what does not exist internally.
mn22:22.1: Monks, would you cling to any possession that is permanent, lasting, eternal, not subject to change, and would remain thus forever?
mn22:22.2: Do you see, monks, any such possession that is permanent, lasting, eternal, not subject to change, and would remain thus forever?”
mn22:22.5: I too, monks, do not see any such possession that is permanent, lasting, eternal, not subject to change, and would remain thus forever.
mn22:23.1: Monks, would you cling to any doctrine of self that, when clung to, would not give rise to sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair?
mn22:23.2: Do you see, monks, any such doctrine of self that, when clung to, would not give rise to sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair?”
mn22:23.5: I too, monks, do not see any such doctrine of self that, when clung to, would not give rise to sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair.
mn22:24.1: Monks, would you rely on any view that, when relied upon, would not give rise to sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair?
mn22:24.2: Do you see, monks, any such view that, when relied upon, would not give rise to sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair?”
mn22:24.5: I too, monks, do not see any such view that, when relied upon, would not give rise to sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair.
mn22:25.1: If there were a self, monks, would there be something belonging to my self?”
mn22:25.3: If there were something belonging to a self, monks, would there be my self?”
mn22:25.5: Since, monks, neither self nor anything belonging to a self can be found as truly and really existing, is not this view:
mn22:25.6: ‘This is the self, this is the world; after death I shall be permanent, lasting, eternal, not subject to change, and I shall remain thus forever’—
mn22:25.7: is this not, monks, a completely and utterly foolish doctrine?”
mn22:25.8: “How could it not be, venerable sir? It is indeed, venerable sir, a completely and utterly foolish doctrine.”
mn22:26.4: And is that which is impermanent painful or pleasant?”
mn22:26.6: And is it fitting to regard that which is impermanent, painful, and subject to change as:
mn22:26.7: ‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self’?”
mn22:26.15: And is that which is impermanent painful or pleasant?”
mn22:26.17: And is it fitting to regard that which is impermanent, painful, and subject to change as:
mn22:26.18: ‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self’?”
mn22:27.1: Therefore, monks, any form whatsoever—past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near—all form should be seen as it really is with right wisdom thus: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.’
mn22:27.5: any consciousness whatsoever—past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near—all consciousness should be seen as it really is with right wisdom thus: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.’
mn22:28.1: Seeing thus, monks, a learned noble disciple becomes disenchanted with form, disenchanted with feeling, disenchanted with perception, disenchanted with formations, disenchanted with consciousness.
mn22:29.1: Being disenchanted, he becomes dispassionate; through dispassion, he is liberated; when liberated, there is knowledge: ‘I am liberated.’
mn22:29.2: He understands: ‘Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more coming to any state of being.’
mn22:30.1: This, monks, is called a monk who has lifted the crossbar, who has filled in the moat, who has pulled out the stake, who is without bolts, a noble one with banner lowered, burden dropped, unfettered.
mn22:31.1: And how, monks, is a monk one who has lifted the crossbar?
mn22:31.2: Here, monks, a monk has abandoned ignorance, cut it off at the root, made it like a palm stump, obliterated it so that it is no longer subject to future arising.
mn22:31.3: Thus, monks, a monk is one who has lifted the crossbar.
mn22:32.1: And how, monks, is a monk one who has filled in the moat?
mn22:32.2: Here, monks, a monk has abandoned the round of births leading to renewed existence, cut it off at the root, made it like a palm stump, obliterated it so that it is no longer subject to future arising.
mn22:32.3: Thus, monks, a monk is one who has filled in the moat.
mn22:33.1: And how, monks, is a monk one who has pulled out the stake?
mn22:33.2: Here, monks, a monk has abandoned craving, cut it off at the root, made it like a palm stump, obliterated it so that it is no longer subject to future arising.
mn22:33.3: Thus, monks, a monk is one who has pulled out the stake.
mn22:34.1: And how, monks, is a monk one who is without bolts?
mn22:34.2: Here, monks, a monk has abandoned the five lower fetters, cut them off at the root, made them like a palm stump, obliterated them so that they are no longer subject to future arising.
mn22:34.3: Thus, monks, a monk is one who is without bolts.
mn22:35.1: And how, monks, is a monk a noble one with banner lowered, burden dropped, unfettered?
mn22:35.2: Here, monks, a monk has abandoned the conceit ‘I am,’ cut it off at the root, made it like a palm stump, obliterated it so that it is no longer subject to future arising.
mn22:35.3: Thus, monks, a monk is a noble one with banner lowered, burden dropped, unfettered.
mn22:36.1: When a monk’s mind is thus liberated, monks, even the devas with Indra, with Brahmā, with Pajāpati, searching, do not find:
mn22:36.2: ‘This is what the Tathāgata’s consciousness depends on.’
mn22:36.4: I say, monks, that even in this very life, a Tathāgata cannot be found.
mn22:37.1: Though I speak and explain thus, monks, some recluses and brahmins wrongly, falsely, vainly, and baselessly misrepresent me, saying:
mn22:37.2: ‘The recluse Gotama is an annihilationist; he teaches the annihilation, destruction, and non-existence of an existing being.’
mn22:37.3: As I am not, monks, and as I do not speak, so those recluses and brahmins wrongly, falsely, vainly, and baselessly misrepresent me, saying:
mn22:37.4: ‘The recluse Gotama is an annihilationist; he teaches the annihilation, destruction, and non-existence of an existing being.’
mn22:37.5: Both formerly and now, monks, I teach only suffering and the cessation of suffering.
mn22:37.6: If others, monks, revile, abuse, provoke, or harass the Tathāgata, there is no resentment, dissatisfaction, or disturbance in the mind of the Tathāgata.
mn22:38.1: If others, monks, honor, respect, revere, or venerate the Tathāgata, there is no delight, joy, or elation in the mind of the Tathāgata.
mn22:38.2: If others, monks, honor, respect, revere, or venerate the Tathāgata, the Tathāgata thinks thus:
mn22:38.3: ‘Such actions are done toward that which I have fully understood.’
mn22:39.1: Therefore, monks, if others revile, abuse, provoke, or harass you, you should not harbor resentment, dissatisfaction, or disturbance in your mind.
mn22:39.2: Therefore, monks, if others honor, respect, revere, or venerate you, you should not harbor delight, joy, or elation in your mind.
mn22:39.3: Therefore, monks, if others honor, respect, revere, or venerate you, you should think thus:
mn22:39.4: ‘Such actions are done toward that which we have fully understood.’
mn22:40.1: Therefore, monks, abandon what is not yours;
mn22:40.2: what you abandon will lead to your benefit and happiness for a long time.
mn22:41.1: And what, monks, is not yours?
mn22:41.2: Form, monks, is not yours; abandon it;
mn22:41.3: abandoning it will lead to your benefit and happiness for a long time.
mn22:41.4: Feeling, monks, is not yours; abandon it;
mn22:41.5: abandoning it will lead to your benefit and happiness for a long time.
mn22:41.6: Perception, monks, is not yours; abandon it;
mn22:41.7: abandoning it will lead to your benefit and happiness for a long time.
mn22:41.8: Formations, monks, are not yours; abandon them;
mn22:41.9: abandoning them will lead to your benefit and happiness for a long time.
mn22:41.10: Consciousness, monks, is not yours; abandon it;
mn22:41.11: abandoning it will lead to your benefit and happiness for a long time.
mn22:41.13: if someone were to carry away, burn, or do as they please with the grass, sticks, branches, and leaves in this Jeta’s Grove, would it occur to you:
mn22:41.14: ‘This person is carrying us away, burning us, or doing as they please with us’?”
mn22:41.17: “Because, venerable sir, that is neither our self nor what belongs to our self.”
mn22:41.18: “In the same way, monks, abandon what is not yours;
mn22:41.19: what you abandon will lead to your benefit and happiness for a long time.
mn22:41.20: And what, monks, is not yours?
mn22:41.21: Form, monks, is not yours; abandon it;
mn22:41.22: abandoning it will lead to your benefit and happiness for a long time.
mn22:41.26: consciousness, monks, is not yours; abandon it;
mn22:41.27: abandoning it will lead to your benefit and happiness for a long time.
mn22:42.1: Thus, monks, the Dhamma has been well-expounded by me, clear, open, evident, and free from patchwork.
mn22:42.2: In this Dhamma, monks, that is well-expounded, clear, open, evident, and free from patchwork, those monks who are arahants, with taints destroyed, who have lived the holy life, done what had to be done, laid down the burden, reached their own goal, destroyed the fetters of existence, and are completely liberated through final knowledge, for them there is no cycle of existence to be described.
mn22:43.1: Thus, monks, the Dhamma has been well-expounded by me, clear, open, evident, and free from patchwork.
mn22:43.2: In this Dhamma, monks, that is well-expounded, clear, open, evident, and free from patchwork, those monks who have abandoned the five lower fetters are all spontaneously reborn, attaining final Nibbāna there, not returning from that world.
mn22:44.1: Thus, monks, the Dhamma has been well-expounded by me, clear, open, evident, and free from patchwork.
mn22:44.2: In this Dhamma, monks, that is well-expounded, clear, open, evident, and free from patchwork, those monks who have abandoned the three fetters, with greed, hatred, and delusion diminished, are all once-returners, returning once to this world to make an end of suffering.
mn22:45.1: Thus, monks, the Dhamma has been well-expounded by me, clear, open, evident, and free from patchwork.
mn22:45.2: In this Dhamma, monks, that is well-expounded, clear, open, evident, and free from patchwork, those monks who have abandoned the three fetters are all stream-enterers, no longer subject to downfall, assured, destined for enlightenment.
mn22:46.1: Thus, monks, the Dhamma has been well-expounded by me, clear, open, evident, and free from patchwork.
mn22:46.2: In this Dhamma, monks, that is well-expounded, clear, open, evident, and free from patchwork, those monks who are Dhamma-followers and faith-followers are all destined for enlightenment.
mn22:47.1: Thus, monks, the Dhamma has been well-expounded by me, clear, open, evident, and free from patchwork.
mn22:47.2: In this Dhamma, monks, that is well-expounded, clear, open, evident, and free from patchwork, those who have even a measure of faith in me, a measure of affection, are all destined for heaven.”
mn22:47.3: This is what the Blessed One said.
mn22:47.4: Delighted, those monks rejoiced in the Blessed One’s words.
mn22:47.5: The Discourse on the Simile of the Snake is concluded, the second.
